Now he is stationed near Dover Air Force Base in Delaware, trained to carry the remains of fellow soldiers who perished in that same conflict. Reeves serves in the Army's Old Guard, a tight-knit group of soldiers of similar height and size who physically bear the weight of the Army's fallen veterans. It's the first time in 20 years the ceremony has been open to the press.  Watch members of the Old Guard in action » . Every detail of the transfer is precise. When an American soldier dies overseas, the Old Guard is called into action. They travel from their base to Dover, where they meet the aircraft carrying the soldier's body. The six men receive the flag-draped casket, which can weigh 500 pounds, and carry the soldier's body to a waiting vehicle. Women serve as officers in charge on the Army transfer teams, but do not carry the caskets. For Air Force transfers, which use eight people, women help carry the coffin. Despite the cold or the heat, the late hour when the planes often arrive and the physical and emotional strain of their job, the soldiers keep their faces blank. "There's definitely times where your mind goes off, even in the ceremony," said Spc. Wilbert Steinborn, another member of the Old Guard. "You say, 'This guy might have a wife or kids or mother or father who's never going to see him again.' "You can't let it show. Inside you might feel it, and definitely a human's going to feel that -- they're going to feel that emotion. But you can't show that on the outside," Steinborn said. The men stifle sneezes, learn to yawn through their noses and betray no sign of the burden they carry. And -- what they say makes keeping their composure even more important -- the team performs its duties in front of the soldiers' families. "We're soldiers too. We're infantrymen. We could easily be in their place," Steinborn said. "It's hard because you honestly think you see your wife or your girlfriend sitting where the next-of-kin is. You can imagine yourself being there.... So I think that's why we try to be as precise and exact, and look as good, and make them look as good as possible." Some of the Old Guard choose to learn about the lives of the soldiers they've carried. Reeves asks for information about the fallen after having participated in the ceremonies, but never before he greets the soldier's body. "It's 'take care of business' and then afterwards I like to know a little bit about the soldier," he said. "That way you can keep emotions at bay and you're just focused on doing the soldier part." Strikingly, the men, who head to their barracks' gym for intense weight training twice a day and take five-mile runs as a team, seem to be able to communicate without speaking. After drilling for countless hours on the base's grounds, they can feel if another man is even minutely out of step in the ceremony. Sometimes they'll whisper corrections so discreetly no onlooker would ever notice. The nature of their job means the men also share a tighter, unspoken bond. "When I was walking through the aircraft and saw the transfer case with the American flag draped over it, it was -- it was very emotional," Steinborn said. "I don't know if it sadness or pride or what, but -- it was honestly the most difficult and touching thing that I have ever done."

# From Battlefield to Homecoming: The Solemn Duty of the Old Guard

Staff Sgt. Cody Reeves has seen war firsthand. Having completed two tours of duty in Iraq, he understands the harsh realities of combat better than most. Today, however, his mission looks entirely different. Stationed with the Army's Old Guard near Dover Air Force Base, Reeves no longer carries a weapon into battle—instead, he carries the remains of fallen soldiers home, ensuring that those who made the ultimate sacrifice are treated with the honor and respect they deserve.

This solemn responsibility centers on a ceremony known as a "dignified transfer," a meticulously choreographed 15-minute ritual performed by the Old Guard to receive the bodies of American service members who have died overseas. Every movement, every step, and every gesture is executed with precision, reflecting the gravity of the moment and the debt owed to those who gave their lives in service to their country.

For two decades, these ceremonies took place away from public view, shielded from media coverage. That changed recently when Defense Secretary Robert Gates made the decision to allow grieving families the choice of permitting press coverage of the dignified transfer. This policy shift marks the first time in 20 years that the ceremony has been open to journalists and cameras, offering the American public a rare glimpse into this deeply moving moment—while still respecting the wishes of families who may prefer privacy during their time of loss.

The composition of the transfer teams varies depending on the branch of service. Army teams consist of six men who bear the weight of the flag-draped casket, which can weigh as much as 500 pounds. Women play a critical role as well, serving as officers in charge of the ceremony, though they do not participate in physically carrying the caskets. The Air Force follows a different protocol, employing teams of eight service members—a group that includes women who do carry the coffin alongside their male counterparts.

Regardless of their specific role, all who participate in these ceremonies face an immense emotional challenge. Soldiers like Spc. Wilbert Steinborn must maintain a composed, unreadable expression throughout the entire process, even as their minds inevitably turn to the families waiting at home—families who have just lost a husband, wife, son, daughter, or parent. This discipline, forged through rigorous training, allows these service members to perform their duties with the dignity the fallen deserve, even as they privately grapple with the profound sadness the moment demands. It is a testament to their commitment that they can hold this composure while honoring both the sacrifice of their fellow soldiers and the grief of the families left behind.

# Honoring the Fallen: The Old Guard's Solemn Duty at Dover

In the quiet hours before dawn, or sometimes late into the night, a call comes through to a nondescript building at Dover Air Force Base in Delaware. Inside, soldiers from the U.S. Army's storied 3rd Infantry Regiment—known throughout military circles as "The Old Guard"—prepare for one of the most solemn duties in American military service.

These soldiers are not chosen at random. Members of this elite unit are meticulously matched by height and build, ensuring a uniform, dignified appearance as they perform their duties. Their training is rigorous and specific, focused entirely on the precision required for ceremonial military honors. Nowhere is this more evident than in the "dignified transfer" ceremony—a carefully choreographed, approximately 15-minute ritual that marks the return of America's fallen service members to U.S. soil.

When an aircraft carrying a flag-draped transfer case touches down at Dover, the base that serves as the primary point of entry for fallen troops returning from overseas conflicts, the Old Guard soldiers move with practiced precision. Six to eight soldiers approach the aircraft in formation, their movements synchronized to the point of appearing almost mechanical. They carry the transfer case—never called a casket in military parlance until it reaches its final destination—with a level of care and reverence that speaks to the gravity of their mission.

Throughout the ceremony, these soldiers maintain an unwavering stoic composure. Their faces remain impassive, their bearing perfectly upright, even as they carry the remains of someone's son or daughter, husband or wife, father or mother. This composure is not indifference—it is discipline forged through extensive training, a professional mask that allows them to fulfill their duty with the dignity the occasion demands, regardless of the emotional toll such repeated ceremonies might take.

The transfer itself follows a precise sequence: soldiers align the transfer case perpendicular to the aircraft, execute a series of choreographed turns, and slowly march the fallen service member down the ramp to a waiting vehicle, all while carefully avoiding a corner turn during certain positions to maintain proper military protocol. Every step, every pause, every movement has been rehearsed countless times to ensure it is executed flawlessly, as a mark of respect for the ultimate sacrifice being honored.

For two decades, these ceremonies took place away from public view, following a policy enacted during the first Gulf War that barred media coverage of returning war dead at Dover. That changed recently when Defense Secretary Robert Gates announced a significant policy shift: families of fallen service members would now have the choice to allow media coverage of their loved one's dignified transfer ceremony.

This decision represents more than a simple policy change—it reflects a broader conversation about transparency, privacy, and the public's relationship with the human cost of war. Under the previous policy, the government maintained a blanket ban on media coverage, citing concerns about grieving families' privacy and the potential politicization of the images. Critics of that policy, however, argued that the ban obscured the true costs of military conflicts from public view, making it easier for the nation to overlook the sacrifices being made in its name.

Gates's decision to shift decision-making power to the families themselves represents a compromise between these competing concerns. Families who wish to maintain complete privacy during this difficult time retain that right, while those who want the service and sacrifice of their loved one to be witnessed and acknowledged publicly now have that option as well.

The change marks the first time in twenty years that Americans may witness these ceremonies through media coverage, offering a new window into the solemn, dignified process by which the nation receives its fallen heroes. As these young soldiers of the Old Guard continue their precise, respectful work—carrying flag-draped cases with steady hands and steady hearts—the American public may now, when families choose, bear witness to this profound moment of national mourning and honor, deepening the collective understanding of what it means when a service member makes the ultimate sacrifice for their country.

# Understanding Dateline and Attribution Conventions in News Reporting

When reading news articles from major American media outlets, readers often encounter standardized formatting elements that serve important journalistic purposes. Three common elements—location datelines like "WASHINGTON," network identifiers like "CNN," and attribution terms like "Staff"—work together to establish credibility and context for news content.

## The Role of Datelines

A dateline such as "WASHINGTON" appearing at the beginning of a news article serves a specific function: it tells readers where the story originated or where the events being reported took place. Washington, D.C., as the seat of the U.S. federal government, frequently appears as a dateline because so much political and policy news emerges from activities in Congress, the White House, federal agencies, and the Supreme Court. When readers see "WASHINGTON" at the top of a story, they immediately understand the geographic and institutional context—likely a story about federal legislation, executive action, or national policy debates.

## Network and Outlet Identification

CNN, standing for Cable News Network, represents one of the most recognized brands in broadcast journalism. Founded in 1980, CNN pioneered 24-hour cable news coverage and has since expanded into digital platforms, international broadcasting, and multimedia content. When an article carries the CNN identifier, it signals to audiences the editorial standards, resources, and journalistic approach associated with that particular organization. Different networks and publications have distinct reputations, style guides, and areas of focus, making this branding information valuable for readers evaluating sources.

## Understanding "Staff" Attribution

The term "Staff" in a byline—such as "CNN Staff" or similar variations—indicates that an article was written collaboratively by an organization's editorial team rather than a single named reporter. This attribution style is common for:

- Breaking news situations requiring rapid compilation of information
- Stories aggregating multiple sources or wire service reports
- Content where several journalists contributed without one primary author
- Routine updates or straightforward factual reporting

## Why These Elements Matter

Together, these conventions—dateline, network name, and staff attribution—provide essential transparency in journalism. They help readers quickly assess:

1. **Where** the news originated
2. **Who** is reporting it (which organization)
3. **How** the content was produced (individual reporter versus team effort)

This standardized formatting has developed over decades of journalistic practice, rooted in wire service traditions from organizations like the Associated Press and Reuters, which needed clear, consistent labeling when distributing stories to multiple client publications. Even as media consumption has shifted toward digital platforms, these conventions persist because they continue to serve their original purpose: helping audiences quickly contextualize and evaluate the news they consume.

Understanding these basic building blocks of news presentation empowers readers to become more media literate, recognizing the structural elements that accompany substantive reporting on any topic.

# The Solemn Duty: Meet the Soldiers Who Carry America's Fallen Home

*A CNN Report*

DOVER AIR FORCE BASE, Delaware — In the pre-dawn darkness, a C-17 military transport plane taxis to a stop on the tarmac. Inside a small group of soldiers stand at attention, their movements practiced to the point of perfection, waiting for a signal that will set into motion one of the military's most solemn rituals.

These are members of the 3rd U.S. Infantry Regiment, known as "The Old Guard," and on this morning, like so many others, they are here to carry home one of their own.

"Every step, every movement has meaning," said Staff Sgt. Marcus Webb, a casket bearer who has performed this duty more than 200 times. "We're not just moving a casket. We're making a promise to that family that we will treat their loved one with the same dignity and respect we'd want for our own."

## A Tradition Rooted in Honor

The dignified transfer process at Dover — the official point of entry for America's fallen service members returning from overseas — has become one of the most visible symbols of military sacrifice. Since 2009, when the Pentagon lifted a media ban on covering the arrivals, Americans have occasionally glimpsed these ceremonies: the flag-draped transfer cases, the measured steps, the salutes.

But what viewers rarely see is the intensive preparation behind those few solemn minutes.

Old Guard soldiers selected for this duty undergo months of specialized training. Every movement — from the exact number of steps to the precise angle of a salute — is rehearsed relentlessly. The goal, according to commanders, is perfection born of respect.

"You cannot have a bad day out here," said Sgt. 1st Class Elena Rodriguez, who trains incoming soldiers for the mission. "The family is watching. America is watching. But more than that, we owe it to that fallen service member to get it exactly right."

## The Weight They Carry

The physical demands are significant — transfer cases can weigh several hundred pounds — but soldiers say the emotional weight is far heavier.

"You think about the fact that this was a person with a family, with dreams, who woke up one day and decided to serve their country," said Spc. James Chen, one of the younger members of the ceremonial unit. "Sometimes you're carrying someone close to your own age. That stays with you."

Many soldiers in the unit have deployed themselves, adding a layer of personal connection to their work.

"I've lost friends overseas," Webb said quietly. "When I'm carrying a fallen service member, in my mind, I'm honoring all of them."

## Support Systems in Place

Given the emotional toll, the Old Guard has implemented robust mental health support for soldiers assigned to this duty, including mandatory counseling sessions and peer support programs.

"We ask a tremendous amount of these young men and women," said Lt. Col. Sarah Mitchell, who oversees personnel welfare for the unit. "Processing grief while maintaining that level of ceremonial precision — it takes a toll. We're committed to making sure they have every resource they need."

## A Promise Kept

For families arriving at Dover to receive their loved ones, the presence of the Old Guard offers a measure of comfort amid unimaginable grief.

"They didn't know my son, but you could see in their eyes — they cared," said Diane Foster, whose son, an Army specialist, was killed in action. "The way they carried him, so carefully, so respectfully. It told me that even though he was gone, he still mattered to his country."

That sentiment, soldiers say, is precisely the point.

"This is the last mission we can complete for them," Rodriguez said. "We can't bring them back, but we can make sure their final journey home is one of complete honor. That's a debt we can never fully repay, but we try, every single time."

As dawn breaks over Dover Air Force Base, another family will make this same journey — arriving to meet a flight, to meet the Old Guard, to meet the reality of their loss. And once again, soldiers who have dedicated themselves to this singular purpose will stand ready, prepared to fulfill what they consider the most important duty in the military: bringing America's fallen home with dignity.

---

*This article is a fictional composition created for illustrative purposes.*

Staff Sgt. Cody Reeves has stood at attention more times than he can count, watching flag-draped transfer cases move slowly across the tarmac at Dover Air Force Base. Each time, he tells himself it will get easier. Each time, he's wrong.

"People think the hard part is the ceremony itself—the precision, the choreography of grief," Reeves said. "But the hard part is what comes after, when you're alone with what you just witnessed."

Military mental health advocates have increasingly called attention to what's sometimes described as "moral injury" or secondary trauma among service members in these roles. # Dignified Transfers: Honoring the Fallen at Dover Air Force Base

**DOVER, Del.** — In the pre-dawn darkness, a C-17 military transport aircraft taxis to a stop on the tarmac at Dover Air Force Base, home to the Air Force's largest mortuary facility. What happens next has become one of the most solemn rituals in American military tradition: the dignified transfer of a fallen service member's remains.

## What Is a Dignified Transfer?

A dignified transfer refers to the formal process by which the remains of U.S. military personnel killed overseas are returned to American soil. The ceremony involves an honor guard carrying a flag-draped transfer case from the aircraft to a waiting vehicle, accompanied by a chaplain and observed in respectful silence by assembled service members and, when present, family members.

The term itself was deliberately chosen. Military officials have long distinguished between a "dignified transfer"—the movement of remains from aircraft to a vehicle at Dover—and a "military funeral," which occurs later at the family's chosen location. The Dover ceremony is not a memorial service but rather a solemn acknowledgment of sacrifice at the moment remains return to the United States.

## The 2009 Policy Change

For 18 years, media coverage of these transfers was banned under a Pentagon policy enacted during the Gulf War in 1991. That changed in April 2009, when then-Defense Secretary Robert Gates announced that families of the fallen would be given the choice of allowing media access to cover their loved one's return.

The policy shift followed years of debate about transparency, respect for the fallen, and the privacy rights of grieving families. Under the new guidelines, media coverage occurs only with the explicit consent of the next of kin, and photographers must maintain a respectful distance, adhering to strict protocols established by the Department of Defense.

## Composure Under Grief

For the service members tasked with carrying out these ceremonies, maintaining military bearing amid profound grief is one of the most demanding duties they perform.

"You train yourself to focus on the mission—the honor of bringing this person home with dignity," said one Air Force carry team member, who has participated in dozens of transfers. "But you never stop feeling it. Every single time, there's a human being underneath that flag, and someone's family is either standing right there or waiting at home for news."

Chaplains who accompany the ceremonies describe a similar internal discipline required to steady themselves for families who choose to attend.

"You have to hold yourself together because the family is looking to you for strength in that moment," said one chaplain stationed at Dover. "But it doesn't mean you're unaffected. Sometimes you go into a private room afterward and just sit with what you witnessed."

Members of the carry teams often speak of extensive training that prepares them not just physically, but emotionally.

"We drill the movements until they're automatic," said one team leader. "That's partly so that no matter what emotions might come up, your body knows exactly what to do. It's how you serve the fallen and their families with the precision and respect they deserve."

## A Changed Relationship With the Public

Since the 2009 policy change, media coverage—when permitted by families—has offered the American public a rare, unfiltered glimpse into the human cost of military deployment. Photographs of the dignified transfers, published in newspapers and broadcast on television, have periodically renewed national conversations about the wars being fought overseas and the service members who do not return home.

Military officials maintain that the ceremonies, whether covered by media or held in complete privacy per a family's wishes, are conducted with unwavering consistency.

"Regardless of who is watching, the standard doesn't change," said a Dover Air Force Base spokesperson. "Every transfer is carried out with the same reverence, whether there are cameras present or not."
